scenes.tts: The double helix revealed the shape of D N A. But how can scientists read base order when shape does not show it? Move the yellow lens to order.
scenes.caption: The double helix revealed the shape of DNA. But how can scientists read base order when shape does not show it? Move the yellow lens to order.
scenes.narration: The double helix revealed the shape of DNA. But how can scientists read base order when shape does not show it? Move the yellow lens to order.
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's 16:9 world without a reset. Reuse the exact colour map: DNA base blocks BLUE; backbones and outlines GREY; question lens YELLOW; shown features GREEN; omitted features ORANGE; evidence PURPLE. The opening DNA sample box and four question frames remain. The yellow lens leaves 'shape' and slides onto 'order'. The rectangular shape card dims behind an ORANGE mask while a BLUE letter strip brightens. Everything remains labelled 'schematic'.
The title 'How DNA Became Readable' appears above the carried order frame. The yellow lens glides along the BLUE letter strip while all other frames drift faintly behind it.

scenes.tts: Start with one template strand. A copying enzyme moves along it, adding matching base blocks. Ordinary blocks let the copy keep growing. The letters are still hidden in the process.
scenes.caption: Start with one template strand. A copying enzyme moves along it, adding matching base blocks. Ordinary blocks let the copy keep growing. The letters are still hidden in the process.
scenes.narration: Start with one template strand. A copying enzyme moves along it, adding matching base blocks. Ordinary blocks let the copy keep growing. The letters are still hidden in the process.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the order frame. A long GREY track labelled 'template' spans the screen with unlettered BLUE base blocks; their identities stay hidden until the readout in the reveal. A rounded PURPLE copier, labelled 'copying enzyme', travels left to right. Matching BLUE blocks click into a new row beneath it. The copy extends smoothly while a small ORANGE cover hides the final readout lane.

scenes.tts: Sanger's original method ran a separate reaction for each kind of base. Each reaction mixed ordinary blocks with a small amount of one kind of stop block. When a stop block joins a copy, that copy cannot grow farther. Many copies grow at once, so copies stop at many different matching positions. Later versions give each kind of stop block its own color and use one reaction.
scenes.caption: Sanger's original method ran a separate reaction for each kind of base. Each reaction mixed ordinary blocks with a small amount of one kind of stop block. When a stop block joins a copy, that copy cannot grow farther. Many copies grow at once, so copies stop at many different matching positions. Later versions give each kind of stop block its own color and use one reaction.
scenes.narration: Sanger's original method ran a separate reaction for each kind of base. Each reaction mixed ordinary blocks with a small amount of one kind of stop block. When a stop block joins a copy, that copy cannot grow farther. Many copies grow at once, so copies stop at many different matching positions. Later versions give each kind of stop block its own color and use one reaction.
scenes.visual: Four reaction trays sit side by side, labelled A, T, G and C on screen only. In each, many identical templates grow copies at the same time; nothing rewinds or repeats. Most incoming blocks are ordinary BLUE blocks; only a few are ORANGE stop blocks, and each tray's stop blocks carry only that tray's letter. Wherever a stop block locks onto a growing row, that copy stops and drops into its tray. Many copies stop at the same position, and each tray fills with BLUE strips of varied lengths, each capped ORANGE. On the last sentence, a small inset labelled 'later versions' shows one tray with four differently coloured stop blocks.

scenes.tts: Each tray now holds a mixture, not one planned staircase. Each copy ends with the base that stopped it. Sorting lanes can turn those lengths into readable order.
scenes.caption: Each tray now holds a mixture, not one planned staircase. Each copy ends with the base that stopped it. Sorting lanes can turn those lengths into readable order.
scenes.narration: Each tray now holds a mixture, not one planned staircase. Each copy ends with the base that stopped it. Sorting lanes can turn those lengths into readable order.
scenes.visual: Shake the trays gently so the copies overlap in a realistic mixture. Then each tray tips its copies into the top of its own tall GREY sorting lane, labelled with that tray's letter. A covered readout waits beside the lanes; strips continue bobbing at the entrances.

scenes.tts: Predict before the lane runs. Which copy reaches the bottom first: a shorter copy or a longer copy? Hold the picture and choose.
scenes.caption: Predict before the lane runs. Which copy reaches the bottom first: a shorter copy or a longer copy? Hold the picture and choose.
scenes.narration: Predict before the lane runs. Which copy reaches the bottom first: a shorter copy or a longer copy? Hold the picture and choose.
scenes.visual: Place one short BLUE strip and one long BLUE strip side by side at the sorting-lane entrance. A yellow question mark appears between them. Text asks 'Which reaches the bottom first?' The copier and remaining strips keep a faint ambient bob.
Deliberate predict pause. The two strips remain at the entrance. The yellow question mark pulses slowly and the sorting lane shimmers faintly. No strip moves downward yet.

scenes.tts: All the copies start moving together, but shorter copies move faster. The shortest reaches the bottom first, then longer copies follow. Reading each stop base in that order reveals the complementary sequence, one position after another.
scenes.caption: All the copies start moving together, but shorter copies move faster. The shortest reaches the bottom first, then longer copies follow. Reading each stop base in that order reveals the complementary sequence, one position after another.
scenes.narration: All the copies start moving together, but shorter copies move faster. The shortest reaches the bottom first, then longer copies follow. Reading each stop base in that order reveals the complementary sequence, one position after another.
scenes.visual: Release the lanes. All strips start moving at the same moment; shorter strips travel faster, so they spread out by length. The shortest strip reaches the bottom first, then strips of increasing length arrive. As each arrives, its lane letter slides into the covered readout. The cover lifts gradually to reveal one growing BLUE letter string. Green checks mark the correct order.

scenes.tts: Sequencing changes the useful model. A coiled shape becomes a letter string. That string shows identity and order clearly, while hiding shape, size, and the partner strand.
scenes.caption: Sequencing changes the useful model. A coiled shape becomes a letter string. That string shows identity and order clearly, while hiding shape, size, and the partner strand.
scenes.narration: Sequencing changes the useful model. A coiled shape becomes a letter string. That string shows identity and order clearly, while hiding shape, size, and the partner strand.
scenes.visual: The completed BLUE readout stretches across the frame. Behind it, the first film's rectangular shape card shrinks and transforms into the same letter strip; no molecule is drawn. GREEN tabs mark 'identity' and 'order'. An ORANGE curtain closes over three labels: 'shape', 'size', 'partner strand'.

scenes.tts: A genome is all the D N A in one chromosome set. A reference sequence acts like a ruler. New sequence strips align against it, making differences easier to find.
scenes.caption: A genome is all the DNA in one chromosome set. A reference sequence acts like a ruler. New sequence strips align against it, making differences easier to find.
scenes.narration: A genome is all the DNA in one chromosome set. A reference sequence acts like a ruler. New sequence strips align against it, making differences easier to find.
scenes.visual: The letter strip lengthens and becomes a wide BLUE ruler labelled 'reference sequence'. Several shorter strips slide underneath and align. Matching positions glow GREEN; differing blocks pulse YELLOW. A tag reads 'comparison standard'. No person icon owns the ruler, preventing a one-person implication.

scenes.tts: The Human Genome Project used improved Sanger sequencing to build a human reference. It joined work from several donors and still left gaps. Later projects filled more gaps and added variation.
scenes.caption: The Human Genome Project used improved Sanger sequencing to build a human reference. It joined work from several donors and still left gaps. Later projects filled more gaps and added variation.
scenes.narration: The Human Genome Project used improved Sanger sequencing to build a human reference. It joined work from several donors and still left gaps. Later projects filled more gaps and added variation.
scenes.visual: The reference ruler assembles from PURPLE donor strips, each labelled only 'donor', with one contribution visibly larger but no invented percentage spoken. Several GREY gaps remain. A timeline appears with all dates shown only on screen from the lesson. Later long strips bridge gaps, and varied strips fan beneath the ruler.

scenes.tts: Reading also became far less costly. Plot the lesson's production-cost estimates on a logarithmic scale. The computed curve plunges, then flattens.
scenes.caption: Reading also became far less costly. Plot the lesson's production-cost estimates on a logarithmic scale. The computed curve plunges, then flattens.
scenes.narration: Reading also became far less costly. Plot the lesson's production-cost estimates on a logarithmic scale. The computed curve plunges, then flattens.
scenes.visual: Transform the reference ruler into the horizontal axis of a full-frame plot. Compute every point directly from the lesson's cost table. Label only the two end years, 2001 and 2022, on the horizontal axis, and the vertical axis 'estimated production cost, log scale'; do not label individual dates or mark any single interval, so the lesson's own predict question about the largest fall stays open. A BLUE curve draws through the points. No decorative or invented data appear.

scenes.tts: The curve needs limits. These are production estimates, not prices paid by a person. Later estimates use an existing reference. Earlier estimates priced building without one. Interpretation costs are excluded.
scenes.caption: The curve needs limits. These are production estimates, not prices paid by a person. Later estimates use an existing reference. Earlier estimates priced building without one. Interpretation costs are excluded.
scenes.narration: The curve needs limits. These are production estimates, not prices paid by a person. Later estimates use an existing reference. Earlier estimates priced building without one. Interpretation costs are excluded.
scenes.visual: Keep the computed curve visible. Split its background into two zones labelled 'build without reference' (earlier) and 're-sequence against reference' (later), with no dates on the boundary. Three ORANGE limit tags attach to the axis: 'production estimate', 'not a customer price', and 'interpretation excluded'. The curve continues a slow tracing glow.

scenes.tts: Lower cost means a fixed budget can read more genomes. Biologists can compare many people and species instead of relying on one reference. The reference remains a model with limits.
scenes.caption: Lower cost means a fixed budget can read more genomes. Biologists can compare many people and species instead of relying on one reference. The reference remains a model with limits.
scenes.narration: Lower cost means a fixed budget can read more genomes. Biologists can compare many people and species instead of relying on one reference. The reference remains a model with limits.
scenes.visual: The plot shrinks to the upper left. One BLUE reference ruler remains across the center while many varied sequence strips align beneath it. A fixed PURPLE budget token stays the same size as the number of readable strips grows. GREEN difference markers appear, while an ORANGE 'leaves out variation' tab stays on the reference.

scenes.tts: Shape required a structure model. Order required a sequence model. Comparison required a reference. Choose D N A models by the question; every model leaves features out.
scenes.caption: Shape required a structure model. Order required a sequence model. Comparison required a reference. Choose DNA models by the question; every model leaves features out.
scenes.narration: Shape required a structure model. Order required a sequence model. Comparison required a reference. Choose DNA models by the question; every model leaves features out.
scenes.visual: Return to the first film's DNA sample box and question frames. The rectangular shape card enters 'shape', the letter strip enters 'order', and the reference ruler enters a new 'comparison' frame. Each carries an ORANGE 'leaves out' tab. The yellow lens moves across all three and stops at the question itself.
End card shows one line only: 'Choose DNA models by the question; every model leaves features out.' The sequence strips and yellow lens continue a slow drift behind the dimmed card.
